content: The document begins with an introduction to the consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in June 2013. These guidelines provide recommendations for a public health approach to managing HIV. The publication emphasizes that the designations and material presented do not imply any legal or territorial opinions by WHO. It also clarifies that the mention of specific companies or products does not constitute endorsement by WHO. The guidelines outline the importance of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in achieving viral suppression and preventing HIV transmission. ART involves the use of a combination of three or more antiretroviral drugs, typically as lifelong treatment. The document highlights the public health approach, which focuses on addressing the health needs of populations rather than individuals. This approach includes simplified drug regimens, free access to care, decentralization of services, and integration of care delivery. Key definitions are provided for terms such as HIV, ART, and populations affected by HIV. HIV refers to the human immunodeficiency virus, with two types: HIV-1, which is responsible for most global infections, and HIV-2. Populations are categorized into adults (over 19 years), adolescents (10–19 years), children (under 19 years), and infants (under one year). Key populations include those most at risk, such as men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, people who inject drugs, and sex workers. Vulnerable populations include groups like adolescents, orphans, street children, and prisoners. The guidelines also address HIV testing and prevention strategies. Voluntary counseling and testing are emphasized, adhering to the principles of consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct test results, and connection to care. Provider-initiated testing is recommended in clinical settings but must remain voluntary. Combination prevention strategies, which integrate behavioral, biomedical, and structural approaches, are encouraged to maximize the impact on reducing HIV transmission. The document discusses the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. It recommends lifelong ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, regardless of their clinical stage or CD4 count. This approach, previously referred to as Option B+, aims to protect both maternal health and prevent vertical transmission of HIV. The guidelines also provide detailed recommendations for monitoring and evaluation, implementation based on local contexts, and dissemination of information. They include algorithms for treatment recommendations for adults, adolescents, pregnant women, and children, as well as tools for early infant diagnosis and readiness assessments for ART implementation. Acknowledgments are given to various contributors, including co-chairs, methodologists, and members of guideline development groups. These individuals represent a wide range of organizations, countries, and expertise, reflecting the collaborative effort behind the development of these guidelines. External peer reviewers and observers are also recognized for their contributions to ensuring the quality and comprehensiveness of the guidelines.
